Why Tide Pools Keep Their Own Weather

By Marguerite Okafor · June 2, 2026

At low tide on a clear morning, the rocky shelf below Bodega Head splits into dozens of small, self-contained worlds. Each tide pool holds its own temperature, its own oxygen level, and its own light regime, shaped as much by the shape of the rock basin as by the ocean outside it. Walk from one pool to the next and you cross, in the space of a few steps, what amounts to a different climate zone.

The pools nearest the high-tide line are stranded longest between inundations, sometimes for twelve hours at a stretch. Left alone under a summer sun, a shallow pool can climb past 28 degrees Celsius even when the open ocean nearby sits at 13. Evaporation concentrates the salt left behind, and by late afternoon a high pool can be measurably saltier than seawater, a condition biologists call hypersalinity. Animals that live there year-round have to tolerate both extremes on the same afternoon.

Lower pools, by contrast, are refreshed by waves every few minutes even at low tide, and their conditions track the ocean far more closely. This vertical gradient, from the splash zone down to the pools that are barely ever dry, is why tide pool guides organize species lists by zone rather than by location alone. A hermit crab common six feet up the shore is often entirely absent six feet closer to the waterline, and vice versa.

Oxygen behaves just as unevenly. During the day, the algae and surfgrass lining a sunlit pool photosynthesize hard enough to push dissolved oxygen well above saturation, sometimes visible as a faint stream of bubbles clinging to the fronds. At night, with photosynthesis stopped and respiration continuing, the same pool can swing toward hypoxia before the tide returns. Sculpins and other pool-resident fish have been shown to gulp air at the surface during these overnight troughs, an ordinary behavior that would look alarming out of context.

Color plays a role too. Darker basalt basins absorb more solar radiation than pale sandstone ones a few meters away, so two pools of identical depth and volume can differ by several degrees purely because of the rock they sit in. Naturalists doing repeat surveys learn to note substrate color alongside depth, since it predicts thermal behavior better than location on the shore chart does.

None of this variability is unique to Northern California, but it is unusually easy to observe here because the tidal range is large and the intertidal shelf is broad and gently sloped rather than a narrow fringe. Similar dynamics have been documented from Maine to the Salish Sea, and the general pattern — small basins decoupling from the surrounding ocean during emersion — shows up in tide pool research from Australia and South Africa as well.

For visitors, the practical upshot is timing. A pool that looks static at 9 a.m. can be a different chemical environment by 1 p.m., which is one reason field guides recommend photographing a pool with a timestamp if you plan to return to the same spot later in the day. It also explains why two people describing "the same" tide pool an hour apart sometimes seem to be talking about different places entirely.
